{{Short description|Framework in formal semantics and logic}}
'''Alternative semantics''' (or '''Hamblin semantics''') is a framework in [[formal semantics (natural language)|formal semantics]] and [[logic]]. In alternative semantics, expressions [[denotation|denote]] ''alternative sets'', understood as sets of objects of the same [[type theory|semantic type]]. For instance, while the word "Lena" might denote Lena herself in a classical semantics, it would denote the singleton set containing Lena in alternative semantics. The framework was introduced by [[Charles Leonard Hamblin]] in 1973 as a way of extending [[Montague grammar]] to provide an analysis for [[questions]]. In this framework, a question denotes the set of its possible answers. Thus, if <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are [[proposition]]s, then <math>\{P,Q\}</math> is the denotation of the question whether <math>P</math> or <math>Q</math> is true. Since the 1970s, it has been extended and adapted to analyze phenomena including [[focus (linguistics)|focus]],<ref name="Krifka1993">{{cite journal | first=Manfred |last=Krifka | title=Focus and presupposition in dynamic interpretation |year=1993 | journal=Journal of Semantics | volume=10 | number=4 | pages=269–300| doi=10.1093/jos/10.4.269}}</ref> [[scope (formal semantics)|scope]],
